sections.title: Proof of Work
sections.tagline: Three things that hold across every seat.

cards.title: Regulated digital assets, from the inside
cards.text: At Grayscale (2024 to 2025) I owned the investor-facing platform for a launch of 10 regulated digital-asset investment products, about $7B. Every release passed product, engineering, legal, risk and compliance, and I cut the release cycle 35%.

cards.title: Zero to one, more than once
cards.text: Co-founded a direct-to-consumer company, $0 to profitable in 24 months ($2M+). As GM, turned a video ad network from $4,500 to over $1M a month and recruited its first CTO; acquired by Meredith. Since 2025, ARCS, built alone.

cards.title: The kill call comes first
cards.text: Tested three AI health product lines for Twill Health; two went forward and one did not. ARCS does this by default: it records what a team expects before a decision and checks it against what happened.

blocks.text: **Not onchain.** ARCS receipts live in Postgres, not on a chain. Onchain is a thesis I have not tested.

blocks.text: Your Idea Engine post: agents write memos six times faster, but not always usable ones. Each use below aims at that gap.

cards.title: An alpha engine
cards.ref: Built: the record and the recheck. Not shown yet: that it beats judgment alone.
cards.text: Much of a studio's edge hides in what it passed on. ARCS records why each hatch was passed and checks it again as the market moves, so a pass that was wrong becomes a lead instead of a loss.

cards.title: A risk-adjusted pipeline
cards.ref: Built: a conviction score on every decision. Not shown yet: how accurate it is.
cards.text: Each hatch carries what the team expects, how sure it is, and what would kill it, so the pipeline reads by risk as well as by excitement.

cards.title: An anti-fragile test bench
cards.ref: Built: pre-registered tests, run once, failures published. Not shown yet: a kill test run on a Gravity hatch.
cards.text: Every kill test is written down before it runs, so a failed test still pays: the next thesis starts from what it ruled out.

head: You ask for
What I bring
rows: Early-stage startup experience
Co-founder, 2012 to 2016 ($0 to profitable in 24 months). GM of a turnaround, 2010 to 2012 ($4,500 to over $1M a month, acquired).
Crypto experience, a thesis not a meme
At Grayscale I owned the investor-facing platform for a launch of 10 regulated digital-asset investment products, about $7B. Mentor at Outlier Ventures (2024).
PM instincts: the riskiest assumption, a spec an engineer can ship
Embedded product partner since 2020 across health, government and media ventures. Three product lines tested, two taken forward.
A working prototype built with Claude Code or Cursor

[RFP-O-Matic](https://github.com/flashesofbrilliance/rfp-engine), a public repo started 2026-11-02. It answers questions about a request for proposal and cites the exact clause, or says the document does not cover it.
Where the AI got it wrong

Agents reported my quality gates green while running a stale copy of the checker from another branch, so a layout bug shipped repeatedly. I now make every gate run from the branch it is checking, and the fix is itself a check.
A high kill rate

In October I pre-registered a retrieval benchmark, ran it once, published every result including the failures, and merged the one change that passed. The beliefs I have overturned are on a [public ledger](https://status.arcs.care/beliefs), each with the test that overturned it.

cards.title: Receipts for agent spend
cards.text: When an AI agent can move stablecoins for a company, every send is final. Wallet policy engines log which rule allowed a send. They do not log what the agent expected or whether it came true. That gap is the wedge.

cards.title: First user, and why it is not built
cards.text: The treasury or compliance lead at a fintech piloting agent payments. ARCS has the receipt and the one-way-door check but no payment rails and no design partner, and your stealth agentic stablecoin payments company may already own this ground. I would ask first.

cards.title: Kill it if
cards.text: Fewer than 3 of 15 teams piloting agent payments say the approval trail is what keeps them from going live.

blocks.text: I commit when an idea passes the kill criteria I wrote in week one and a named design partner agrees to a pilot. If nothing survives by month six, you get the written kills. At one in thirty, those are data, not waste.

tabs.headline: Open Application: choose your own adventure.
tabs.lede: Your open application asks what I would own that you don't staff today, and why you'd move faster with me. My answer: a hatch desk, sketched to build with you, in the open.

blocks.text: Most funds call it a deal desk or a platform role. I would run it as an AI-native platform team whose work compounds, owning the hatch pipeline: each memo, its kill criteria, the record of every call.

Every pass is logged with its reasons and rechecked as the market moves. A wrong pass surfaces before you miss the next one like it, and each thesis starts from what the last 29 taught. The call stays yours, and comes faster.
It sits on top of your Idea Engine: the agents find and draft, the desk keeps the record. Nothing gets built twice.
